messages.subject: merging pull/88?

Was there anything else I needed to do for that?

Looks like Ben says it compiles with C++11 now:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/pull/88#issuecomment-18517933

The above comment also mentions a separate issue with Boost
local, which is a separate issue. I still don't think this
is our issue, but we should try to isolate it and add it
to the ongoing issues they're having with references to
temporaries, some of which seem to occur only at higher
optimization levels:

https://svn.boost.org/trac/boost/ticket/5190

https://svn.boost.org/trac/boost/ticket/6126

https://svn.boost.org/trac/boost/ticket/8489

- Bob

On Thursday, May 30, 2013 2:09:17 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Was there anything else I needed to do for that?

Looks like Ben says it compiles with C++11 now:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/pull/88#issuecomment-18517933

The above comment also mentions a separate issue with Boost
local, which is a separate issue.  I still don't think this
is our issue, but we should try to isolate it and add it
to the ongoing issues they're having with references to
temporaries, some of which seem to occur only at higher
optimization levels:

https://svn.boost.org/trac/boost/ticket/5190

https://svn.boost.org/trac/boost/ticket/6126

https://svn.boost.org/trac/boost/ticket/8489

So, after the merge, it does indeed work for clang++ with -std=c++11 and O_STANC=0 (the default). And, as we know, stanc doesn't work for clang++ with -std=c++11 and O_STANC>0. However, I was surprised to find that stanc also doesn't work for g++-4.8 with --std=c++11 and O_STANC=0. The failures messages (attached) for the latter two cases when doing make test/gm/parser are a bit different, suggesting that there is some undefined behavior going on here. However, adding -fsanitize=undefined in the clang++ case didn't flag anything.

Ben

I haven't even read up on C++99 vs. C++11, but I believe
some behaviors have changed in the language and in the libs.

The Boost grammars are really pushing on the language, especially
in terms of lambda-like lazy evaluation.

> However, I was surprised to find that stanc also doesn't work

This could also be a bug on their side.

We really should track all this down if we're going to push
Stan as an API. As a built-in to something like R, it's less
of an issue because we have more control over compilation flags.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: merging pull/88?
parts:
Was there more context here as to which class I should
be looking at? I'm just not sure any of this is under
our control.

I also seem to recall there being some differences in
the specs for iterators in C++11 around return-by-reference
and return-by-value:

https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups#!topic/comp.std.c++/f0CdiAZAl_Y

You can see that the reference type changed between C++98 and
C++11 here:

http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/iterator/istreambuf_iterator/

In C++11, it's charT&, whereas in C++98, it was just charT.
I wish they'd have defined operator* more precisely like they
did for everything else. I'm guessing it may return a reference
type. So I'm guessing this example:

charT operator*() const { return sbuf_->sgetc(); }

would be this in C++11:

charT& operator*() const { return sbuf_->sgetc(); }

which would cause a problem by returning a reference to
a local [namely the return of sbuf_->sgetc()].

- Bob

This still looks to me like it's a problem with the
character iterators --- that's the position_begin and
position_end business.

The align error
> align_ = <Unable to determine byte size.>

appears to come from here:

https://llvm.org/svn/llvm-project/lldb/trunk/source/Core/Value.cpp

I have no idea how to debug this. I'm still not convinced this
is our doing and not an issue with the iterators and how their
return type changed from value to reference in C++11.

I'll try to create a small reproducible error and see if I
can get a response from the Spirit list. I didn't get an answer
about the unsequenced question. I can try stackoverflow, too.

- Bob
